pages.summary: Fit a polynomial by least squares; coefficients from the highest power down.
body: Finds the polynomial of degree `n` that passes closest to the points, in the sense of the smallest sum of squared differences. The coefficients come highest power first, ready for `polyval` and `roots`. With `mu`, x is centred and scaled first (`(x - mu(1))/mu(2)`), which keeps a high degree well conditioned; `S` holds what `polyval` needs for error estimates.
syntax: The coefficients of the degree `n` polynomial.
With a structure for `polyval`'s error estimates.
Fitted to centred and scaled x: `mu` is `[mean(x); std(x)]`.
inputs: x, y — vectors of the same length
The degree. With `n + 1` points the polynomial passes through every one.

body: The polynomial `p(1)*x^n + p(2)*x^(n-1) + … + p(n+1)` at each element of `x`, by Horner's rule. The coefficients come highest power first, as `polyfit` gives them.
syntax: The polynomial at each element of `x`.
For coefficients fitted to centred and scaled x (`polyfit`'s `mu`).
With the standard error of each prediction, from `polyfit`'s `S`.

body: The values where the polynomial is zero, found as the eigenvalues of its companion matrix: a column of `n` roots for a polynomial of degree `n`, complex where they are. The coefficients come highest power first; `poly` goes the other way.

body: Each element of the result is a sum of products of `u` and `v` slid past each other. For coefficient vectors this multiplies the polynomials; for a signal and a filter's weights it filters the signal. The full result has `length(u) + length(v) - 1` elements; `'same'` keeps the central part the size of `u`.
syntax: The central part the size of `u`, or only the parts computed without padding.

body: Given values `v` at points `x`, estimates the values at other points `xq`. `'linear'` (the default) joins the points with straight lines; `'spline'`, `'pchip'` and `'makima'` use smooth cubic pieces (pchip and makima do not overshoot the data); `'nearest'`, `'previous'` and `'next'` copy a neighbour's value. Points outside the data give `NaN` unless `'extrap'` or a value is given.
syntax: Extending the method beyond the data.
vq = interp1(x, v, xq, method, extrapval)
inputs: The points, all different (sorted or not).
The values; a matrix has a column for each set of values.

The methods side by side

pages.summary: A cubic spline (not-a-knot ends, or clamped when two more values are given).
body: A smooth curve of cubic pieces through the points, with continuous first and second derivatives. At its ends the first two pieces (and the last two) are one cubic (not-a-knot), unless `y` has two more values than `x`: then the first and last are the slopes at the ends (clamped). With two inputs it gives the piecewise polynomial for `ppval`.
syntax: The spline as a piecewise polynomial.

examples.title: Through a few points of a sine
Clamped ends
examples.intro: Two extra values give the slopes at the ends: here zero at both. The curve leaves its first point flat instead of rising steeply.

pages.summary: An integral by the trapezoidal rule.
body: Sums the areas of trapezoids under the points: for points `x` and values `y`, `sum(diff(x) .* (y(1:end-1) + y(2:end)) / 2)`. It integrates sampled data, such as measurements; for a function that can be evaluated anywhere, `integral` is more accurate. Without `x` the spacing is 1.
syntax: At the points `x` (or with the scalar spacing `x`).

examples.title: The area under a sampled curve
examples.code:
x = linspace(0, pi, 50);
Q = trapz(x, sin(x))

pages.summary: A definite integral, by adaptive quadrature.
body: Integrates a function from `a` to `b` to about ten significant digits, splitting the interval where the function is hard. The function must accept a vector and return a vector of the same size, so write it with element-wise operators (`.*`, `./`, `.^`). The limits may be `Inf`.
syntax: q = integral(fun, a, b, 'RelTol', r, 'AbsTol', t)
For a function that returns an array for a scalar.
Splitting the interval at `w` (for jumps or kinks).

examples.title: A polynomial and a Gaussian
examples.code:

q = integral(@(x) exp(-x.^2), -Inf, Inf)
sqrt(pi)

pages.summary: A root of a function of one variable.
body: Finds a point where the function crosses zero, starting from a guess `x0` or from an interval `[a b]` where the function changes sign (then a root inside it is certain). It needs a sign change: a root where the function only touches zero, as `x^2` at 0, is not found.
syntax: A root in an interval where `fun(a)` and `fun(b)` have opposite signs.
With options from `optimset`, such as `'TolX'` or `'Display'`.
With the value there, how it ended (1 when it found a root) and a summary.

examples.title: A root in an interval, and the value there

pages.summary: The minimum of a function of several variables, by the Nelder-Mead simplex (no derivatives).
body: Searches from the start point `x0` by moving a simplex of points downhill. It needs no derivatives and copes with a function that is not smooth, but it finds a local minimum, close to the start, and is slow for many variables. The function takes a vector the shape of `x0` and returns a number.
syntax: With the function's value at the minimum, how it ended and a summary.

examples.intro: The parameters of y = a*exp(-b*t) that make the squared misfit smallest.

pages.summary: The minimum of a function of one variable on an interval.
body: Searches between `a` and `b` by golden section and parabolic steps. It finds a local minimum inside the interval (or an end, if the function falls toward it).
syntax: With the function's value there, how it ended and a summary.

examples.title: The lowest point of a curve
The largest area of a rectangle in a semicircle
examples.intro: Minimizing the negative area maximizes the area: a rectangle of half-width x under the unit semicircle has area 2*x*sqrt(1 - x^2).

pages.summary: Solve a nonstiff ODE system y' = f(t, y) by the Dormand-Prince Runge-Kutta pair of orders 5 and 4: the first solver to try.
body: Steps from the initial values `y0` over `tspan`, choosing step sizes to keep the estimated error within tolerances. `odefun(t, y)` returns the derivatives as a column. With `tspan` of two values the solution comes at the steps taken; with more values, at those times. For stiff problems (very different time scales) use `ode15s`.
syntax: Times as a column, and the solution with a row for each time.
With options from `odeset`, such as `'RelTol'` and `'AbsTol'`.
The solution as a structure for `deval`.
inputs: `@(t, y) ...` returning a column the length of `y0`.

examples.title: Exponential decay, against the exact solution
examples.code:
[t, y] = ode45(@(t, y) -2*y, [0 3], 1);
maxError = max(abs(y - exp(-2*t)))
plot(t, y, 'o-')
xlabel('t')
ylabel('y')
